root.note: Through Vulgar Latin *iānuella ‘little door’, a reconstructed diminutive.

history: A Portuguese window is a little door. Latin iānua meant ‘door’, and spoken Latin made a diminutive, *iānuella, ‘small door’. In the west of Iberia that small door became the opening in the wall for light and air: Old Portuguese janella, today janela. Iānua belongs with Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who looked both ways, and with January, the month that opens the year, in Portuguese janeiro. Other languages chose other images. Spanish ventana is a ‘wind opening’, from ventus, and English window is Old Norse ‘wind eye’. When booking a seat on a plane or a comboio, ask for janela or corredor, ‘aisle’.
historyEinfach: Janela means ‘window’. It comes from Latin and means ‘little door’. The month janeiro, January, comes from the same Latin family: the god Janus was the god of doors. Spanish ventana and English window come from words for ‘wind’.

elsewhere.text: Galician, the closest neighbour, has the same little door.
English named the window after the wind, like Spanish ventana.
